paras: The attempted lynching of Will Roseboro took place at Statesville, Iredell County, North Carolina, on August 2, 1903, when crowds gathered to seize a Black prisoner accused of assaulting and murdering a white woman, Mrs. Dolph Beaver. Sheriff W. A. Summers kept him from the crowds and took him to Charlotte; Roseboro was later tried, convicted and hanged. Papers outside the state cited the sheriff's conduct as a sign of a "reaction against lynching," while a Raleigh correspondent reported that many leading citizens sympathized with the crowd.

Mrs. Beaver's body was found in a well at her home in Cool Springs township after her husband returned from Statesville. A coroner's jury found that she had been choked, struck on the head and "outraged," and charged Wilford Roseboro, "colored," a neighbor. Summers arrested him on August 1 near Melrose in Polk County.

According to the News and Observer's Salisbury correspondent, about six hundred people, most from Cool Springs, watched incoming trains on Saturday and Sunday "for the purpose of capturing the negro culprit and lynching him." Summers left the train west of Statesville and brought Roseboro into the jail by a back way at 10:40 Sunday morning. The correspondent wrote that "it is reported" a small group of bystanders tried to take the prisoner, and that Summers drew his pistol and dispersed them.

At 2 p.m. Summers slipped Roseboro out by private conveyance to Mooresville and took a train to Charlotte. About 5 o'clock a crowd of several hundred went to the jail, and the deputy in charge let some of them search it in vain. The Associated Press told a shorter story, in which Summers eluded "the gathering mob" before reaching Statesville.

Roseboro was held in the Mecklenburg jail until August 11, when he was returned to Statesville for trial. Before the trial, according to the Statesville Landmark, Solicitor Hammer "submitted some remarks on lynching" to impatient spectators. A jury convicted Roseboro of first-degree murder in twenty-three minutes, and Judge Allen sentenced him to hang.

The News and Observer reported that Roseboro confessed to a Black minister, the Rev. A. J. Arthur, that he choked Mrs. Beaver after a quarrel in her orchard. He was hanged at the Statesville jail on September 10, when the crowd tore away the canvas enclosure and about 2,000 people watched. His relatives refused the body, which was sent to Raleigh for dissection. No report of arrests among the crowds appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press account ran on August 3 under headlines such as "ESCAPED LYNCHING" and "MOB HAD FORMED TO LYNCH A NEGRO," with the Kennebec Journal calling Roseboro a "Negro Ravisher." The Butte Inter Mountain placed the mob in Asheville.

The News and Observer's special, reprinted in Richmond, ran as "LYNCHING WAS NARROWLY AVERTED." It praised Summers's "fine piece of official work" while calling Roseboro "the negro who brutally assaulted and afterwards murdered" Mrs. Beaver before any trial. It also reported elite sympathy for a crowd "prepared to do the work without disguise."

The Montgomery Advertiser quoted the New York Evening Post placing Summers "on the new roll of honor." The Salt Lake Herald remarked that the sheriff who "sneaked away" had denied constituents "the pleasure of lynching," and a Nebraska weekly noted a sheriff who jailed his prisoner "before the lynchers could string him up."
The only Black-press item found, a one-line Savannah Tribune brief of September 19, reported the execution without mentioning the crowds.

The AP said Summers eluded the mob before reaching Statesville, while the News and Observer said he held Roseboro in the Statesville jail for hours and faced a reported seizure attempt there. An Asheville special dated August 3 said Roseboro had been taken secretly to the Asheville jail. The coroner's jury found an assault, but the reported confession described only choking, and the headline said Roseboro "Says Nothing of Darker Crime Charged."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Will Roseboro
bases: Crowds of several hundred gathered at Statesville to seize and lynch a jailed Black man accused of murder; a small group reportedly tried to take him from the sheriff and a crowd searched the jail, but no one was killed (A12, A5).

The crowds that sought Roseboro (about 600 watching trains, several hundred at the jail) acted without authority over an accusation of assault and murder, but the sheriff kept him from them and he was not killed by a mob (A12, A5); he was later hanged after a trial and sentence (A27, A32).

The Associated Press dispatch from Charlotte and the News and Observer's separate Salisbury correspondent agree that a crowd formed at Statesville to lynch Roseboro and that Sheriff Summers evaded it and took him to Charlotte (A5, A7, A12), though they differ on details (A6, A13).

accounts.label: Associated Press wire (Charlotte)
accounts.gist: A mob began forming at Statesville as the sheriff's train approached; Summers eluded it, drove to Mooresville and took Roseboro to the Charlotte jail.

accounts.label: News and Observer correspondent (Salisbury)
accounts.gist: About 600 people watched trains; Summers jailed Roseboro at Statesville by a back way, reportedly drew his pistol on bystanders who tried to take him, removed him at 2 p.m., and a crowd searched the jail at 5 p.m.

accounts.label: Asheville special
accounts.gist: Roseboro was brought secretly to the Asheville jail because officers feared Cool Springs citizens would lynch him.

accounts.label: Statesville special (inquest)
accounts.gist: The coroner's jury charged Roseboro; he was taken to the Charlotte jail Sunday evening and feeling against him was very high.

accounts.label: New York Evening Post (via Montgomery Advertiser)
accounts.gist: Summers saved the accused by taking him to Charlotte and keeping off would-be lynchers at pistol point.

accounts.label: Roseboro's reported confession
accounts.gist: Roseboro told a Black minister he choked Mrs. Beaver after a quarrel in her orchard; he said nothing of an assault.

News and Observer 'LYNCHING WAS NARROWLY AVERTED' praised the sheriff yet called Roseboro the man who 'brutally assaulted and afterwards murdered' her and reported elite sympathy for the crowd.
New York Evening Post via Montgomery Advertiser put Summers on 'the new roll of honor' as a sign of 'reaction against lynching'.
Salt Lake Herald quip that the sheriff 'sneaked away' and denied constituents 'the pleasure of lynching'.
The Frontier noted a sheriff who jailed a Black prisoner 'before the lynchers could string him up'.
